SECTION 010:00–4:21

Equal rows expose the earlier basis error

Row dependence and column dependence meet in the rank.

Strang opens by correcting the proposed basis from the previous lecture. The vectors u = (1, 1, 2)ᵀ and v = (2, 2, 5)ᵀ are independent, but adding w = (3, 3, 8)ᵀ does not give a basis for R³.

M=[123123258]

The first two rows are identical, so M cannot be invertible. Its first and third rows are independent, making its row space two-dimensional. Its column space also has dimension 2, so the three columns are dependent.

The dependence can be checked directly:

w = −u + 2v,   or u − 2v + w = 0.

The important new connection is that row information can reveal column information. The two spaces need not contain the same vectors, but their dimensions are always equal.

Correction carried forward. Lecture 9’s reading edition already marked this slip. Here the lecturer explicitly corrects it. The displayed relation is an editorial check of the corrected conclusion.

SECTION 024:21–8:28

Name all four fundamental subspaces

The transpose turns rows into columns and supplies the fourth space.

An m × n matrix A comes with four fundamental subspaces. The first two are familiar:

C(A) = {Ax : x ∈ Rⁿ},
N(A) = {x ∈ Rⁿ : Ax = 0}.

The row space contains all combinations of A’s rows. To keep using column vectors, transpose each row. These become the columns of Aᵀ, so the row space is written C(Aᵀ).

C(Aᵀ) = {Aᵀy : y ∈ Rᵐ}.

Transposition also supplies another nullspace:

N(Aᵀ) = {y ∈ Rᵐ : Aᵀy = 0}.

This is the left nullspace of A. Its vectors describe combinations of A’s rows that give the zero row, just as N(A) describes combinations of columns that give the zero column.

All rows span the row space, but they are a basis only if independent. As with the column space, a spanning list may contain redundant vectors.

SECTION 038:28–11:44

Place the spaces in Rⁿ and Rᵐ

Count components before comparing vectors or spaces.

A column of A has m entries; a row has n. The equation Ax = 0 uses n unknowns, while Aᵀy = 0 uses m. Thus the spaces split into two ambient spaces:

IN Rⁿ

C(Aᵀ) and N(A)

Row combinations and homogeneous input vectors.

IN Rᵐ

C(A) and N(Aᵀ)

Column combinations and left-null vectors.

SHAPE

A is m × n

A maps n-component inputs to m-component outputs.

For the three-by-four example used later, the row-space and nullspace vectors have four components. The column-space and left-nullspace vectors have three.

Equal dimensions do not identify spaces. Row space and column space can even live in different ambient spaces. A drawing organizes their names and component counts; it does not replace their defining equations.

SECTION 0411:44–14:42

Use original pivot columns for the column space

A basis answers both what the space is and how large it is.

To understand each space, Strang asks two questions: how can we construct a basis, and what is its dimension?

For the column space, row reduction identifies the pivot indices. The corresponding columns of the original A are independent and span all columns. They form a basis for C(A).

Basis for C(A): original pivot columns.
dim C(A) = r.

The rank r counts the pivots. Every nonpivot column is a combination of pivot columns; elimination preserves those dependence coefficients.

Do not substitute the pivot columns of the reduced matrix for the original ones. Row operations can change the column space as a set, even though its dimension stays r. The worked example below makes that difference visible.

SECTION 0514:42–17:06

The row space has the same dimension as the column space

Rank counts independent rows as well as independent columns.

The central rank theorem is

dim C(Aᵀ) = dim C(A) = r,
rank(Aᵀ) = rank(A).

The opening example explains why this matters. Two identical rows immediately rule out three independent rows. Since the remaining two distinct rows are independent, the row dimension is exactly 2. The column dimension is therefore also 2.

This theorem applies to rectangular matrices too. It does not assert that row and column spaces are equal; it asserts that their basis sizes are equal.

The row-reduction argument developed shortly will produce r independent nonzero rows spanning the original row space. That proves its dimension is r, matching the number of original pivot columns.

SECTION 0617:06–21:09

Count the two nullspaces by their free variables

The four dimensions are r, n − r, r, and m − r.

We already know how to build a basis for N(A): choose one free variable to be 1 and the others to be 0, then solve for the pivot variables. Repeat for each free variable.

The special solutions are independent because their free-coordinate patterns are distinct coordinate vectors. They span the nullspace because every homogeneous solution is determined by its free values.

dim N(A) = n − r.

Now apply the same reasoning to Aᵀ. This matrix has m columns and the same rank r. Its homogeneous system therefore has m − r free variables:

dim N(Aᵀ) = m − r.
SpaceAmbient spaceDimensionBasis construction
C(A)RᵐrOriginal pivot columns
N(A)Rⁿn − rSpecial solutions of Ax = 0
C(Aᵀ)RⁿrNonzero rows of reduced R, transposed
N(Aᵀ)Rᵐm − rSpecial solutions of Aᵀy = 0, or tracked elimination

The two dimensions in Rⁿ add to n; the two in Rᵐ add to m. The following sections supply the row-space and tracked-elimination basis constructions in detail.

SECTION 0721:09–23:56

Reduce the familiar three-by-four matrix

Two pivots and two free columns emerge from three row operations.

The example returns to the matrix from Lecture 9:

A=[123111211231]

Perform R₂ ← R₂ − R₁ and R₃ ← R₃ − R₁. This leaves

U=[12310−1−100000]

Multiply row 2 by −1 to make its pivot 1. Then subtract twice this new row 2 from row 1:

R=[101101100000]

Columns 1 and 2 are pivot columns, columns 3 and 4 are free, and rank(A) = 2. The zero bottom row reflects the original equality of rows 1 and 3.

We now use A and R for different basis tasks. The original pivot columns give C(A); the nonzero reduced rows give the row space.

SECTION 0823:56–25:24

Row operations preserve the row space, but can move the column space

Equal rank does not mean equal column spaces.

The column spaces of A and R are different. The vector (1, 1, 1)ᵀ is a column of A, but cannot lie in C(R), whose vectors all have third component zero.

More explicitly, the two independent original pivot columns span the plane x = z. The pivot columns of R are e₁ and e₂, which span z = 0:

C(A) = {(t, s, t)ᵀ : t, s ∈ R},
C(R) = {(t, s, 0)ᵀ : t, s ∈ R}.

Both planes have dimension 2, but they are different subsets of R³.

Row space behaves differently. Each new row is a combination of old rows, and every allowed row operation can be reversed. The old rows are therefore also combinations of the new ones. The two row spans are exactly equal.

The homogeneous solution set also stays fixed: Ax = 0 and Rx = 0 are equivalent systems. Thus N(A) = N(R).

Explicit comparison. The lecture supplies the column-space counterexample and the row-space conclusion. The plane equations and nullspace restatement make the preserved and changed sets precise.

SECTION 0925:24–29:48

The nonzero rows of R form a row-space basis

Reversibility proves spanning; pivot positions prove independence.

Read the two nonzero rows of R and stand them up as column vectors:

q1=[1011],q2=[0110]

These are independent: in a combination αq₁ + βq₂, the first component is α and the second is β. A zero vector forces both coefficients to vanish.

They span the row space because row reduction is reversible. Let aᵢ denote the original row i, written as a column. In this example the relations are

q₁ = −a₁ + 2a₂,   q₂ = a₁ − a₂,
a₁ = q₁ + 2q₂,   a₂ = q₁ + q₂,   a₃ = a₁.

Each list is built from the other. The shared row space is

C(Aᵀ) = {(α, β, α + β, α)ᵀ : α, β ∈ R}.

In general, the r nonzero rows of a reduced echelon matrix are independent because of their pivot positions. They span the original row space, so dim C(Aᵀ) = r.

Use the correct source matrix

For a column-space basis, take pivot columns from A. For a row-space basis, take nonzero rows from R and transpose them.

Relations written out. The lecture explains the forward and reverse row operations. The coefficient identities above are their explicit values for this example.

SECTION 1029:48–33:25

A left-null vector annihilates A from the left

Aᵀy = 0 is equivalent to yᵀA = 0.

The fourth space contains vectors y satisfying Aᵀy = 0. Why call it the left nullspace of A?

Transpose the whole equation. A product reverses order under transpose:

(Aᵀy)ᵀ = yᵀ(Aᵀ)ᵀ = yᵀA = 0ᵀ.

The row vector yᵀ now sits on the left of A. Its entries weight the rows of A, and the result is the zero row.

Thus a left-null vector encodes a row dependence. In comparison, a vector in N(A) encodes a column dependence.

The convention in this edition, as in the lecture, is to keep y as a column with m components and define the space using Aᵀy = 0. Its transpose yᵀ has shape 1 × m, so yᵀA has shape 1 × n.

SECTION 1133:25–38:20

Track every row operation beside the identity

The right-hand block records an invertible matrix E with EA = R.

To recover the left nullspace without starting a new reduction of Aᵀ, keep a record of the operations used on A. Append the m × m identity:

[ A | Iₘ ] → [ R | E ].

Apply every operation to the entire augmented row. If their combined effect is multiplication by E on the left, the identity block becomes E and the original block becomes EA. Consequently,

EA = R.

E is invertible because every elementary row operation is reversible. It is an m × m change of rows, even if A is rectangular.

When A is square and invertible, R = I, so EA = I and E = A⁻¹. For a rectangular A, E is still a valid invertible row-operation matrix, but it is not an inverse of A.

Where to stop. Reduce the A block to R and carry those same operations through the identity block. The displayed [R | E] need not be the full reduced echelon form of the entire augmented array: further pivots inside E can change its entries. The board’s E records the stated reduction of A.

SECTION 1238:20–42:33

Read the left-nullspace basis from the zero rows

The matching rows of E are the row-dependence coefficients.

Repeat the three reduction steps on I₃. Subtract row 1 from rows 2 and 3; multiply row 2 by −1; then subtract twice the new row 2 from row 1. The accumulated matrix is

E=[−1201−10−101]

Its product with the original matrix checks the calculation:

EA=[101101100000]

The last row of R is zero. Therefore the last row of E, (−1, 0, 1), gives a zero row combination of A. Transpose it to obtain

y=[−101]

Indeed, yᵀA = −row₁(A) + row₃(A) = 0. Since m − r = 3 − 2 = 1, this single nonzero vector is a basis for N(Aᵀ).

In general, the m − r rows of E corresponding to zero rows of R are independent, since they are a subset of the rows of an invertible matrix. Each annihilates A, so their transposes form a basis for the left nullspace.

For this example all four dimensions are now accounted for: the row space and nullspace in R⁴ have dimensions 2 and 2; the column space and left nullspace in R³ have dimensions 2 and 1.

For reference, the two special solutions of Ax = 0 from Lecture 9 are

s1=[−1−110],s2=[−1001]

Their combinations are (−c − d, −c, c, d)ᵀ, matching every solution of the two reduced homogeneous equations. Together with the original pivot columns, the reduced row basis, and y, they complete the example’s four bases.

General basis argument. The lecture identifies the relevant row of E and states the construction. Independence and the dimension count above explain why the selected rows always form a basis.

SECTION 1342:33–45:14

Matrices themselves can form a vector space

The required operations are addition and scalar multiplication.

In the closing minutes, Strang expands the meaning of a vector. A vector need not be drawn as an arrow or written as a single column. Consider M, the set of all real three-by-three matrices.

The vector-space operations are familiar: add two matrices entry by entry, and multiply every entry by a real scalar. Combinations such as 3P − 5Q stay in M. The zero vector is now the all-zero matrix.

These operations obey the vector-space rules. For example, addition is associative and commutative, the zero matrix leaves P unchanged, and multiplying P by 1 returns P.

The fact that matrices also have a matrix product PQ is irrelevant to this question. A vector space requires addition and scalar multiplication; it does not require a product of two vectors.

The object changes; the definitions stay

Independence, spanning, basis, and dimension apply to lists of matrices using exactly the same linear-combination tests.

SECTION 1445:14–47:27

Upper triangular and symmetric matrices are subspaces

Their intersection consists exactly of diagonal matrices.

Within M, let U contain all upper triangular three-by-three matrices and S contain all symmetric three-by-three matrices.

Both sets contain the zero matrix. Adding upper triangular matrices leaves zeros below the diagonal, and scalar multiplication preserves them. Adding symmetric matrices preserves Pᵀ = P, and scalar multiplication does too. Thus both are subspaces.

What belongs to their intersection? An upper triangular matrix has zero entries below its diagonal. If it is also symmetric, each matching entry above the diagonal must be zero too. Only the diagonal entries remain free.

U ∩ S = D, the subspace of diagonal matrices.

Conversely, every diagonal matrix is both upper triangular and symmetric, so the equality holds in both directions.

The lecture leaves the upper triangular and symmetric basis counts for the next lecture. It closes by constructing a basis for D.

SECTION 1547:27–49:11

Count basis matrices to find the diagonal dimension

Three independent diagonal directions give dim D = 3.

A diagonal matrix has three freely chosen entries. A convenient basis uses one nonzero entry at a time. In the lecture’s final choice, the diagonal entries are 1, 3, and 7:

D1=[100000000],D2=[000030000],D3=[000000007]

The matrices are independent: if αD₁ + βD₂ + γD₃ is zero, the diagonal entries force α = 0, 3β = 0, and 7γ = 0.

They span D because any diagonal matrix can be written

diag(a, b, c) = aD₁ + (b/3)D₂ + (c/7)D₃.

The three coefficients can choose the three diagonal entries separately. Therefore {D₁, D₂, D₃} is a basis and dim D = 3. Replacing the nonzero 3 and 7 by 1 gives the usual diagonal coordinate basis.
